AUT.story:
Most of the Austrian record concerns children placed in residential homes after 1945 by youth welfare offices, the public services responsible for children whose families were judged unable to care for them. A historians' commission reported in 2012 that roughly 100,000 children passed through Vienna's municipal, church and private homes after 1945, and described sadistic sexual abuse by some staff. At the city's Wilhelminenberg home (1948–1977), a city commission found in 2013 that caregivers and outside men raped and sexually exploited girls as young as about six. A University of Innsbruck study for the states of Tyrol and Vorarlberg found in 2015 that their homes kept children isolated and dependent, and that this system produced and tolerated sexualised violence until the 1980s.

The people responsible for oversight knew of the abuse. The Wilhelminenberg commission found that staff in the supervising city department knew and did not act, and that city politicians who heard of it in the 1960s ignored it. In seven church-run homes in Tyrol, where one nun at Martinsbühel looked after up to 50 girls in the 1970s, former residents told a 2022 commission that state youth welfare and school authorities did not look closely. The Bishop of Innsbruck called the findings a "total pedagogical failure" of church and state.

In the Catholic Church, the Archbishop of Vienna, Cardinal Hans Hermann Groër, stepped down in 1995 after a former pupil accused him of sexual abuse, allegations the bishops later called well founded. In 2010 the bishops set up a victims' commission chaired by Waltraud Klasnic, and by 2021 the church had approved payments in 2,550 cases, about €33 million in total. In October 2025, after a press report, SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich, the Austrian children's villages charity, said there were credible allegations that its founder, Hermann Gmeiner (died 1986), had abused eight boys at four villages; victims had come forward from 2013 and been compensated without the charity making it public. Prosecutors in three cities opened investigations.

Austria's main response has been commissions and compensation, often set up by the institutions concerned. The victims' organisation Weisser Ring, working for the City of Vienna, paid €42.13 million to 2,384 people by 2019; Tyrol and Vorarlberg had compensated 521 people by 2015. The US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 21,366 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse geolocated to Austria in 2024. The US State Department names Austria as a destination for women and girls trafficked from Romania.

The abuse in post-war homes has been documented and partly compensated. The investigations into SOS-Kinderdorf are open.

BIH.story:
The Bosnian record concerns the sexual enslavement of women and girls during the war and their trafficking in the years after it. In both periods, people with official power took part.

During the war, Bosnian Serb forces in the town of Foča held Bosniak women and girls in 1992–93 at detention sites such as the Partizan Sports Hall, next to the municipal police building, and took them from there to flats and houses to be raped. The UN war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) found that these forces used rape as an instrument of terror and that local police guarded the women and joined in their mistreatment. In 2001 it convicted three men, including Radomir Kovač, who held two girls in his flat for about four months and sold victims to other soldiers, and Zoran Vuković, who raped a girl he knew to be 15; Dragoljub Kunarac, a Bosnian Serb army unit leader, received 28 years for torture, rape and enslavement. The sentences were upheld on appeal in 2002.

From 1995, bar owners bought women and girls brought mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine and held them in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Human Rights Watch reported in 2002 that local police acted as owners, guards and clients. Foreign staff of the international mission were also buyers. Eighteen monitors of the UN International Police Task Force (IPTF), which supervised Bosnian police, were sent home after buying women, visiting brothels or facing trafficking-related charges, and Human Rights Watch found none prosecuted. A US Army criminal investigation documented employees of DynCorp, a US company providing civilian contractors to SFOR, the NATO-led peace force, buying women from brothels; they too were sent home, which kept them from being used as witnesses. DynCorp fired IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking; a British employment tribunal found the dismissal unfair.

The foreign buyers were protected by immunity and repatriation, and the local police meant to act against traffickers were among the clients. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) rated the influence of criminal actors inside the Bosnian state at 8 out of 10 in 2025 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 3.88 out of 10. The US State Department rates Bosnia Tier 2, meaning it does not fully meet US minimum standards against trafficking but is making significant efforts.

The wartime crimes at Foča led to convictions at an international court. The record contains no prosecution of the peace-mission staff or contractors who bought women and girls.

CRI.story:
Two forms appear in the Costa Rican record: sex trafficking of children in tourist zones and border areas, and abuse by Catholic clergy.

The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says traffickers subject Costa Rican women and children to sex trafficking, especially in Pacific coastal zones and near the northern and southern borders, where social tolerance makes children more vulnerable. It also identifies girls from Nicaragua, Panama, the Dominican Republic and Venezuela among the victims, so Costa Rica receives children as well as supplying them. The report rates Costa Rica Tier 2, meaning it does not fully meet US minimum standards but is making significant efforts. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scored its human trafficking market at 5.5 out of 10 in 2025. The US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received 21,742 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse geolocated to Costa Rica in 2024, or 423.8 per 100,000 people.

The one church case on record involves a priest who left the country to avoid trial and a hierarchy accused of knowing for years. Mauricio Víquez, a former church spokesman on family issues, fled in 2018 when accusations surfaced, travelling through Panama to Mexico, where he was caught and extradited in 2021. The church expelled him from the clergy in 2019. In 2022 he was sentenced to 20 years for the sexual abuse and rape of an 11-year-old boy in his parish in 2002–2003. A civil court then ordered Archbishop José Rafael Quirós, the Episcopal Conference (the national body of bishops) and the church's property entity to pay 65 million colones, about US$100,000, in damages; the victims' lawyer said the church had known since 2002 and did nothing. Three other complaints were declared time-barred, meaning the legal deadline for bringing them had passed.

Trafficking of children in coastal and border areas is reported as ongoing. With one church case on record, the wider extent of clergy abuse in Costa Rica is not documented here.

EGY.story:
The record for Egypt holds no documented cases of child abuse networks or child trafficking. What it holds are outside ratings and a count of online reports.

The US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), which receives reports of suspected child sexual abuse material from internet companies, received 249,898 reports geolocated to Egypt in 2024, or 214.4 per 100,000 people. Walk Free estimated in 2023 that 442,000 people in Egypt were in modern slavery, a figure covering all ages and all forms, not only children. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scored Egypt's human trafficking market at 6 out of 10 in 2025, the influence of criminal actors inside the state at 8.5 out of 10, and the country's resilience to organised crime at 3.75 out of 10. The US State Department rates Egypt Tier 2, meaning it does not fully meet US minimum standards against trafficking but is making significant efforts.

Childlight, a research centre on child sexual exploitation, found in its 2026 update that the Middle East and North Africa lack representative survey data on online child sexual exploitation, so there is no estimate of how many children in Egypt are affected.

TUN.story:
The record for Tunisia holds no documented cases of child abuse networks or child trafficking. What it holds are outside ratings and a count of online reports.

The US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), which receives reports of suspected child sexual abuse material from internet companies, received 22,449 reports geolocated to Tunisia in 2024, or 182.9 per 100,000 people. Walk Free estimated in 2023 that 27,000 people in Tunisia were in modern slavery, a figure covering all ages and all forms. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scored Tunisia's human trafficking market at 4.5 out of 10 in 2025, the influence of criminal actors inside the state at 6.5, and resilience to organised crime at 4.33. The US State Department places Tunisia on its Tier 2 Watch List, for countries that do not meet its minimum standards and whose efforts it considers at risk of slipping.

Childlight, a research centre on child sexual exploitation, found in its 2026 update that the Middle East and North Africa lack representative survey data on online child sexual exploitation, so there is no estimate of how many children in Tunisia are affected.

GRL.story: The record for Greenland holds no documented cases of child abuse networks or child trafficking. The US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, which receives reports of suspected child sexual abuse material from internet companies, received 382 reports geolocated to Greenland in 2024. Because the population is small, this equals 672.1 reports per 100,000 people. Walk Free estimated 0.6 people per 1,000 in modern slavery, a figure covering all ages and forms. Nothing in this record shows what lies behind the online reports or whether any involve organised networks.

CHL.story:
The Chilean record has four parts: illegal adoption abroad of children of poor mothers, abuse in state child protection, abuse in the Catholic Church, and Colonia Dignidad, a German sect's enclave. In each, a state body or large institution controlled the children and those in charge did not act on reports for years.

From the 1970s to the 1990s, and most under the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990), children were taken from mainly poor, often rural mothers, some of whom were told their babies had died, and sent for adoption in the United States and Europe, including Sweden. A parliamentary commission found in 2019 that hospital staff, Civil Registry staff and paid private intermediaries took part. A judge's criminal investigation, opened in 2018, covers about 8,000 adoptions abroad.

SENAME, the National Service for Minors, ran centres and accredited private homes for children in state care. Family-court judges and UNICEF found in 2012 that sexual abuse was a constant in these homes; in one home in Arica, carers organised the sexual exploitation of girls. The report was held back for four months until the news site CIPER published it in 2013. In 2018 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child found the state responsible for grave violations, including sexual abuse, in SENAME residences over 40 years.

In the Church, superiors protected accused clergy. Parishioners reported Fr Fernando Karadima to Archbishop Fresno in 1984, and Cardinal Errázuriz shelved a credible investigation in 2004–05; the Vatican found Karadima guilty in 2011. Pope Francis defended Bishop Juan Barros, a Karadima protégé, until a Vatican envoy's report led him to admit serious errors in 2018, and every Chilean bishop then offered to resign. In 2019 prosecutors counted 166 investigations of church members, including 10 bishops, and 248 victims, 131 of them children or adolescents.

Paul Schäfer founded Colonia Dignidad in 1961 after fleeing a German warrant for abusing two boys, and drew in local farm children through a free school and clinic. Chilean officials believe Pinochet's secret police, DINA, used the colony to torture opponents. When a teenager fled to the West German embassy in 1966, it reported finding no evidence. An investigation began only in 1997; Schäfer hid in Argentina and was convicted in 2006 of abusing 25 children. The colony doctor, convicted of aiding the abuse, fled to Germany, where prosecutors dropped their own case in 2019.

As of 2023 nobody had been brought to justice for the illegal adoptions. Germany acknowledged its diplomats' failures over Colonia Dignidad in 2016 and announced compensation for victims in 2019.

IDN.story:
Three forms dominate the Indonesian record: foreign men travelling to Indonesia to buy sex with children, the sale of babies abroad, and, in the past, children taken from occupied East Timor.

The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says sexual exploitation of children by foreign offenders is prevalent in the Riau Islands, which border Singapore, and that women and girls are coerced into commercial sex in Batam, one of those islands. In Puncak, near Bogor in West Java, tourists from the Middle East pay more than $700 for week-long "contract marriages", temporary marriages arranged by brokers, with girls as young as nine. The report says the government tacitly accepted this practice and that corruption and official complicity significantly impeded efforts against trafficking. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scored Indonesia's human trafficking market at 7.5 out of 10 in 2025 and the influence of criminal actors inside the state at 8 out of 10.

Babies are sold abroad on forged papers. In July 2025 West Java police said a syndicate of recruiters, caretakers and document forgers had sold at least 25 babies since 2023, mostly to buyers in Singapore, for 11–16 million rupiah each, some reserved before birth. The syndicate prepared false family cards and passports in Pontianak. Police arrested 13 people and asked Interpol to help trace the adopters. Earlier adoption abroad also involved abuses; a Dutch government commission found in 2021 serious violations in adoptions from countries including Indonesia between 1967 and 1997/98.

Indonesia was also the destination for children removed by its own forces. East Timor's truth commission (CAVR) found in 2005 that at least 4,000 children were taken from their families and moved illegally to Indonesia between 1975 and 1999, by military units, some of which used them as child soldiers or servants, and by Islamic organisations that converted them. Many were renamed and lost contact with their families. CAVR and a joint Indonesia–Timor-Leste commission recommended a commission to search for them, and none was created.

Walk Free estimated that 1,833,000 people in Indonesia were in modern slavery in 2023, a figure covering all ages and forms. The US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received 1,181,246 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse geolocated to Indonesia in 2024. The State Department rates Indonesia Tier 2, meaning it does not fully meet US minimum standards but is making significant efforts.

The State Department reports exploitation by foreign visitors in the Riau Islands and Puncak as continuing in 2025. No official search has been made for the children taken from East Timor.

JAM.story:
Two forms appear in the Jamaican record: the sale of children for sex, in tourist resort areas and in some home communities, and the sexual abuse of children in state care.

The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says children are subjected to sex trafficking in resort areas frequented by tourists, sometimes with their parents' involvement, and that in some communities men pay girls or their families for sex. It names family members, "dons" (local strongmen who control some neighbourhoods) and both foreign and local buyers among those involved. A 2023 prevalence study cited in the report estimated that 6.3 percent of Jamaican children aged 12 to 17 had experienced conditions indicating trafficking. The report says endemic corruption and official complicity, including within law enforcement, remained significant concerns. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scored the influence of criminal actors inside the Jamaican state at 7.5 out of 10 in 2025.

Children in the state's own care were also abused, and the agency meant to supervise their homes was not inspecting them. After a public campaign about abuse in children's homes, the government appointed a review panel chaired by Sadie Keating in 2002. Its 2003 report found that children in homes and places of safety, the state's emergency shelters, had been sexually abused, including by care staff. Nine of the 15 homes the panel visited could not recall an inspection by the Child Services Division, the responsible government agency, in the previous three years.

The State Department rates Jamaica Tier 2, meaning it does not fully meet US minimum standards but is making significant efforts. The US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received 10,312 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse geolocated to Jamaica in 2024, or 363.2 per 100,000 people.

The 2025 report describes the sale of children in resort areas as ongoing. The record does not show what changed in state homes after the 2003 review.

KOR.story:
The largest part of the South Korean record is the sending of children abroad for adoption. About 163,898 children were sent between 1953 and 2008, 109,242 of them to the United States and thousands each to France, Denmark, Sweden, Norway and other countries. The rest concerns online abuse run from Korea, the sale of runaway children for sex, Korean buyers abroad, and abuse in institutions.

Four authorised private agencies held guardianship of the children and sent them abroad under government policy. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, a state body that investigates past rights abuses, found in March 2025 that the agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, registered children with known parents as orphans and did not properly obtain consent. It found the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to welfare at home and failed to supervise the agencies. Receiving countries pressed for more children. When South Korea tried to stop adoptions to Scandinavia in 1974, Swedish, Danish and Norwegian diplomats sent nine pleas and adoptions resumed. South Korea set a policy to phase out adoption abroad after a peak of 8,837 children in 1985, yet 18,578 were still sent between 2003 and 2022.

Welcome to Video, a darknet site run by Son Jong-woo, sold access to more than 250,000 abuse videos for Bitcoin; Korean police counted 223 Koreans among 310 users arrested in 32 countries. Son served 18 months in Korea, and the Seoul High Court refused to extradite him to the United States in 2020. On the messaging app Telegram, operators of the "Nth Room" and "Doctor's Room" chatrooms blackmailed women and girls into producing sexual images and sold access to them; the two leaders received 34 and 40 years. In 2024 police handled more than 800 sexual deepfake cases by late September, against 156 in all of 2021, most involving teenagers, often in chatrooms aimed at particular schools.

The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says runaway children are exploited in bars, nightclubs and escort services, and that a police officer was convicted in a 2022 case of alleged complicity. The Korean Institute of Criminology said in 2013 that South Korean men were the main buyers in child sex tourism in Southeast Asia. At the Gwangju Inhwa School for deaf students, a 2005 investigation found six staff had sexually abused at least nine students; two escaped punishment because the legal time limit had passed, and a 2011 law then removed that limit for sex crimes against children under 13 and disabled people.

President Lee Jae-myung apologised for the adoption abuses in October 2025. Laws now punish viewing abuse material and possessing sexual deepfakes, and police deepfake cases rose sharply through 2024.

MAR.story:
The Moroccan record centres on foreign men who come to Morocco to sexually exploit children, and on how the state has treated those it convicted.

The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says some foreign nationals, mainly from Europe and the Middle East, sexually exploit children in major Moroccan cities. Non-governmental organisations report that tourists exploit children in Tangier in holiday rentals owned and managed by Europeans. The report also records alleged exploitation of children after the September 2023 Al Haouz earthquake. Moroccan courts convicted 60 traffickers in 2024, and the report rates Morocco Tier 2, meaning it does not fully meet US minimum standards but is making significant efforts.

Royal pardons have twice freed convicted foreign offenders. Daniel Galván Viña, a retired Spanish professor, was sentenced in 2011 to 30 years for raping 11 Moroccan children aged 4 to 14. In July 2013 King Mohammed VI pardoned him among 48 Spanish prisoners, and he left Morocco on an expired passport with the authorities' knowledge. Police violently dispersed protesters outside parliament in Rabat; the king then revoked the pardon, saying he had not been told the details of the case, and Galván was arrested in Spain. A 2010 US diplomatic cable reported a royal pardon in 2006 of a Frenchman convicted of abusing a 15-year-old boy in Marrakesh. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scored the influence of criminal actors inside the Moroccan state at 7.5 out of 10 in 2025.

Morocco also appears as the home country of accused offenders abroad. UN tables of allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse for 2015–2016 name Moroccan military personnel serving in the UN missions in the Central African Republic and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In adoption, the Flemish government in Belgium stopped adoptions from Morocco after screening every country of origin, a review prompted by malpractice found in adoptions from Ethiopia.

The US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received 130,173 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse geolocated to Morocco in 2024. Childlight, a research centre, found in 2026 that the Middle East and North Africa lack representative survey data on online exploitation.

The State Department describes exploitation by foreign visitors as ongoing in 2025. The number of children affected is not known.

MMR.story:
Myanmar's record is shaped by armed conflict. Soldiers and armed groups abduct and sexually abuse children, and traffickers sell girls displaced by the fighting across the border into China. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) scored Myanmar's human trafficking market at 9 out of 10 in 2025, the influence of criminal actors inside the state also at 9, and resilience to organised crime at 1.46 out of 10. The US State Department rates Myanmar Tier 3, its lowest rating, for countries that do not meet its minimum standards and are not making significant efforts.

In the UN's findings, the armed forces, known as the Tatmadaw, are the main perpetrators. The UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission found in 2018 that hundreds of Rohingya women and girls were raped during the army's 2017 "clearance operations" and that 80 percent of corroborated cases were gang rapes. Its 2019 report called sexual violence a "hallmark" of army operations in Rakhine, Kachin and Shan States, and documented Rohingya men and boys as young as twelve subjected to sexual violence in Buthidaung prison in 2012. In the current fighting, the UN verified the abduction of 85 children in 2024, 41 by the armed forces and allied militias and 33 by the Kachin Independence Army (KIA), an ethnic armed group, mostly to recruit them.

Displacement supplies the trade in "brides". Human Rights Watch reported in 2019 that women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan States, many displaced by the conflict, were sold for US$3,000–13,000 to Chinese families, who locked them up and raped them so they would become pregnant. Traffickers included relatives and acquaintances. Human Rights Watch said authorities in both countries were looking away. The 2025 US report says displaced women and girls in these states remain vulnerable to forced marriage and forced childbearing in China.

Buddhist monasteries, which house many poor children so they can attend school, operate with little outside oversight. TIME reported that up to 300,000 children may live in monasteries, with few records kept. In one case reported by Myanmar Now, four girls aged 10 to 14 said a monastery's administrator monk had raped them repeatedly from 2017; he disappeared when parents went to police, and TIME described police deferring to the religious affairs ministry and the Sangha, the monastic order.

Walk Free estimated 657,000 people in modern slavery in Myanmar in 2023, across all ages and forms. Abductions by armed forces and armed groups, and the sale of displaced girls into China, are reported as continuing.

NLD.story:
The Dutch record has four parts: abuse of children in church, state care and other organisations since 1945; the Netherlands as a destination for children adopted abroad through fraud; Dutch servers hosting abuse material; and the sexual exploitation of Dutch girls inside the country.

Commissions have found that, across institutions, those in charge knew and did not act. The Deetman Commission, set up by the Catholic Church, identified in 2011 at least 800 priests, monks and other religious who abused children between 1945 and 1985, and found bishops and officials followed a policy of "not hanging out the dirty washing". The Samson Commission received 800 claims of sexual abuse in state-arranged care in 2012, 65 percent about children's homes and 30 percent about foster families, and found the government and care services did not do enough. The De Winter Commission confirmed this in 2019 for youth care as a whole. In sport, 70 percent of perpetrators in 686 cases reported from 2001 to 2017 were coaches or supervisors. Among Jehovah's Witnesses, a 2020 government-commissioned study found only 27 percent of cases reached the police, the rest being handled by elders.

As a receiving country, the Netherlands took in children from countries where they were bought, stolen or given false papers. In the 1980s about 4,000 Sri Lankan babies were adopted to the Netherlands, many through "baby farms" where babies bought or taken from hospitals were handed to paid stand-in mothers. Another 4,099 came from South Korea, whose truth commission found in 2025 that agencies registered children with known parents as orphans. The Joustra Commission found in 2021 serious violations in adoptions from Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil, Colombia and elsewhere from 1967 to 1997/98, and that officials had known for years. The government suspended all adoption from abroad that year and announced a ban in 2024.

Dutch hosting companies have held more of the abuse material found by the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF), a British reporting body, than any other country for years, with 47 percent in 2018, falling to 11 percent, or 33,788 web addresses, in 2025. INHOPE, the international network of hotlines, still ranked the Netherlands first in 2025. The Boylover forum, whose owner and server British police traced to the Netherlands, led to 670 suspects and 230 children safeguarded by 2011.

Inside the country, pimps and "loverboys", recruiters who pose as boyfriends, exploit Dutch girls. The National Rapporteur on trafficking estimated in 2017 that at least 1,320 Dutch girls aged 12 to 17 are sexually exploited each year, and reported cases rose from 868 in 2023 to 944 in 2024.

Adoption from abroad has been suspended since 2021, and the Dutch share of hosted material has fallen. Reported exploitation of Dutch girls is rising.

PER.story:
Two forms dominate the Peruvian record: the sexual exploitation of girls and children around mining camps and in tourist areas, and abuse inside Catholic religious groups, above all the Sodalicio de Vida Cristiana, a lay society founded in Lima.

Exploitation follows illegal mining and tourism. In La Pampa, an illegal gold-mining zone in Madre de Dios next to the Tambopata reserve, bars and brothels served the mining camps. When more than 1,500 soldiers and police moved in under a state of emergency in 2019, the Women's Minister said the worst crimes committed there included child sexual exploitation, and her ministry took in minors and women rescued from trafficking. The US State Department's 2025 report says Peruvian, Venezuelan and Bolivian women and girls are lured to mining and logging camps, and that tourists from the US and Europe exploit children in Cusco, Lima and the Amazon. In Loreto, it says, criminal groups take foreign tourists by boat to remote places on the Amazon River where women and children are exploited.

Peru is also a destination on regional trafficking routes. The State Department reports that Tren de Aragua, a Venezuelan criminal organisation with affiliated groups in Peru, used the Colombian border city of Cúcuta to move trafficking victims to Peru. It notes that two Peruvian police officers were charged with crimes against trafficking victims and that corruption remained a significant concern.

In the Church, abuse was handled internally until outsiders exposed it. Journalists Pedro Salinas and Paola Ugaz published abuse by the Sodalicio's founder, Luis Fernando Figari, and his associates in 2015, and faced legal action. In 2017 the group gave prosecutors an expert report on sexual abuse of minors by Figari and four former members. After an investigation by Vatican envoys, the Vatican expelled Figari in 2024 for physical, psychological and sexual violence, including against minors, and suppressed the society in 2025. Religious orders have also moved accused men into and out of Peru. The Marist Brothers moved Brother Abel Pérez from Chile to Peru in 2010 after he confessed to abusing minors, and the Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas went from Lima to Bolivia after first abusing a child in Lima in 1964.

Peruvian courts convicted 59 traffickers in 2024. Adoption abroad remains open, with 2,049 children sent between 2003 and 2022. The US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received 148,686 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse geolocated to Peru in 2024.

Exploitation around mining camps and by foreign tourists is reported as continuing in 2025. The Sodalicio no longer exists.

PSE.story:
The record for Palestine consists of UN findings on sexual violence connected with the war that began in October 2023, and of outside indicators. No cases of child abuse networks or child trafficking are documented here.

The UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel found in June 2024 that Israeli security forces subjected Palestinians to sexual and gender-based violence during arrests and detention, including forced public nudity and sexualised torture, and that "men and boys were targeted in particular ways". It found that the persecution of Palestinian men and boys on grounds of gender amounted to a crime against humanity. The same commission found that Hamas and other armed groups committed sexual violence on 7 October 2023 at the Nova festival, Nahal Oz and several kibbutzim, and took 252 people hostage, 36 of them children. The findings do not give a count of children among the victims of sexual violence.

The US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received 11,187 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse geolocated to Palestine in 2024, or 211.5 per 100,000 people. Walk Free estimated 10 people per 1,000 in modern slavery, across all ages and forms. Childlight, a research centre, found in 2026 that the Middle East and North Africa lack representative survey data on online child sexual exploitation. Palestine announced a ban on the gaming platform Roblox in November 2025, according to Wikipedia, after child-safety concerns in the region.

How many Palestinian children have been sexually abused in detention or exploited online is not known from this record.

SLE.story:
Most of the Sierra Leonean record concerns the civil war, when armed groups abducted girls for sexual slavery and forced marriage and used children as fighters. Two further forms appear around the war: aid workers and peacekeepers taking sex from children in exchange for food and aid, and the adoption abroad of children whose parents had not consented.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2004 that the Revolutionary United Front (RUF), the main rebel group, and the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), a military faction, deliberately set out to abduct and rape girls aged 10 to 14, and in a few cases younger, using them as sexual and domestic slaves and "wives". It found the Civil Defence Forces, the pro-government militias, also followed a deliberate strategy of rape and sexual slavery against girls. The Special Court for Sierra Leone, set up jointly by the UN and the government, convicted three RUF leaders in 2009 of sexual slavery and of forced marriage as a crime against humanity; Issa Sesay and Morris Kallon were also convicted of using child soldiers. In 2012 the same court convicted Charles Taylor, the former president of neighbouring Liberia, of aiding and abetting RUF crimes including sexual slavery and the use of children under 15 as fighters.

Aid itself was used to obtain sex. The truth commission found girls as young as 12 forced to pay for aid with sex. A 2002 report by the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and Save the Children UK said refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were sexually exploited by employees of aid organisations and UN bodies and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food. The UN's internal investigators then examined 43 cases, substantiated 10, and said they found no evidence of "widespread" abuse, a finding Save the Children disputed.

Adoption abroad drew on the same poverty. In 1998 about 29 children at a centre in Makeni run by Help A Needy Child International (HANCI) were taken to Freetown for medical checks and never returned; their parents later learned they had been adopted by Americans. Sierra Leone suspended adoptions in 2009, and in 2012 a presidential commission shut HANCI down, finding that the families "cannot be said to have genuinely consented". In 2023 a commission for the SOS Children's Villages charity named Sierra Leone among countries where it confirmed serious abuse allegations or found failures to report.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scored the influence of criminal actors inside the state at 8 out of 10 in 2025. Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data on online child sexual exploitation for West and Central Africa, so its extent here is not known.

SWE.story:
Most of the Swedish record concerns Sweden as a destination for children adopted from abroad through fraud and coercion. The rest covers abuse and neglect in Swedish children's homes and foster care, unaccompanied migrant children who went missing, and Swedish men who bought or sold abuse material online.

Swedish families adopted children from countries where they had been taken from their parents by the state, by soldiers or by brokers. Sweden received 9,051 South Korean children between 1957 and 2005, from a system that South Korea's truth commission found in 2025 registered children with known parents as orphans. When South Korea tried to stop adoptions to Scandinavia, the Swedish ambassador urged it in January 1975 to keep sending children. Children taken from mainly poor Chilean mothers, some told their babies had died, were adopted in Sweden, most under the Pinochet dictatorship. In Guatemala, a 2009 government archive study found the army and National Police moved children into the adoption system during the war of 1977–1989, and its chief investigator said the children went mainly to the United States, Sweden, Italy and France. Babies from Sri Lankan "baby farms" of the 1980s also went to Sweden. Sweden's own state inquiry reported in June 2025 that, over 65 years, there were numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea.

Inside Sweden, a government inquiry reported in 2011 on abuse and neglect in children's homes and foster care from 1920 to 1980. The government apologised publicly that year, and a compensation board set up in 2013 had decided just over 4,000 applications by July 2015, rejecting 53 percent with no right of appeal. Europol said in 2016 that at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 1,000 of them in Sweden, and that it had evidence some had been sexually exploited.

In online abuse, Swedes appear as sellers and buyers. A Czech photographer who exploited close to 70 socially and financially disadvantaged children distributed the images with a Swedish partner to customers in the EU and Canada; two people were arrested in Sweden in 2014. In 2026 Swedish police were among seven forces that arrested 28 men suspected of paying cryptocurrency for access to dark web forums with abuse videos. The Internet Watch Foundation, a British reporting body, acted on 6,820 web addresses hosted in Sweden in 2025, 2 percent of its total, and the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received 30,068 reports geolocated to Sweden in 2024.

The 2025 inquiry has documented the adoption abuses. What happened to the 1,000 migrant children who disappeared in Sweden is not known from this record.

VAT.story:
The Holy See, the central government of the Catholic Church based in Vatican City, governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. In this record it appears mainly as the authority that set the rules for handling abuse by clergy worldwide, and as a refuge for some accused clerics.

For most of the twentieth century those rules required secrecy. The instruction Crimen sollicitationis of 1962, restating one from 1922, covered church cases of obscene acts with pre-adolescent children and bound tribunal members, accusers and witnesses to absolute secrecy on pain of automatic excommunication. The canon lawyer Thomas Doyle called it a written policy to cover up cases; others argue it did not bar reporting to police. From 2001, all cases of clergy abusing minors went to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, the Vatican office for church discipline, under the "pontifical secret", the highest level of church confidentiality, until December 2019. The Holy See told a UN committee in 2014 that this office had studied 3,420 credible cases from 2004 to 2013 and that 884 priests had been dismissed. National inquiries in Ireland, the United States, Australia, Germany, France and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. In 2014 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child found that the Holy See had put the church's reputation and the protection of offenders above children's interests.

The Vatican also took accused clerics out of the reach of national courts. Its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, was recalled in 2013 before Dominican prosecutors opened an investigation into abuse of minors; he was laicised and indicted in the Vatican, and died before trial in 2015. A Vatican diplomat recalled from Washington, Mgr Carlo Capella, was convicted in 2018 by a Vatican tribunal of possessing and sharing abuse images, and was not tried in the United States or Canada. Ireland's Murphy Commission received no Vatican files. The Vatican sanctioned Bishop Carlos Belo of Timor-Leste in 2020 over allegations of abusing boys but disclosed this only after a magazine reported it in 2022. The Holy See's own 2020 report found that Pope John Paul II made Theodore McCarrick Archbishop of Washington in 2000 despite a written warning; a church court later found McCarrick guilty of sexual offences with minors and adults.

Since 2019 the rules have changed. Pope Francis required clergy to report abuse and cover-ups to church authorities and allowed bishops to be investigated. He lifted the pontifical secret so that information can go to state authorities, and raised the age in the Vatican's definition of child abuse material from 14 to 18.

Church law now lets information on abuse cases go to state authorities, but does not require bishops to report abuse to them.

ZWE.story:
The Zimbabwean record has three parts: the marriage and sexual exploitation of girls in apostolic churches, sex trafficking and child labour around mines, and abuse that reached the country from Britain, through a child migration scheme in colonial Southern Rhodesia and through the evangelical camps of John Smyth.

Apostolic churches, independent Christian movements with large followings, are the largest documented setting. After a 14-year-old girl died in childbirth at a shrine of the Johanne Marange Apostolic Sect in August 2021, the Zimbabwe Gender Commission, a state body, opened a public investigation. It found compulsory virginity testing, the pledging of girls as wives, betrothal and forced marriage in the Marange sect. An earlier probe in 2020, of branches around Marondera, had found girls of about 10 to 15 taken in as "wives-in-waiting" and married at puberty. By 2022 the commission had investigated over 500 cases of child marriage and sexual exploitation, and it called for a law to regulate faith-based organisations.

Poverty and custom make girls available to traffickers and buyers. The US State Department's 2025 report says traffickers exploit women and children for sex around mines, sometimes in exchange for money or food, and that children may be used as panners and ore couriers in gold and diamond mines. It says girls are made vulnerable by families trading daughters for food or money and by ngozi, the practice of giving a relative to another family to atone for a killing, and that low-level official complicity persisted. The report places Zimbabwe on its Tier 2 Watch List. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scored the influence of criminal actors inside the state at 8 out of 10 in 2025.

British institutions sent abuse to the country and did not warn it. Between 1946 and 1956, 276 child migrants from the UK were sent to the Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College; England's child abuse inquiry found that children who told the headmaster a padre had sexually abused them were beaten and warned against "spreading malicious lies". In the 1980s John Smyth, whose beatings of boys at English evangelical camps had been described in a 1982 internal report kept from police, moved to Zimbabwe and in 1986 founded camps for boys there. A 16-year-old died at one of his camps in 1992. He was arrested in 1997 but never charged, and moved to South Africa in 2001. The 2024 Makin Review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa" and found no evidence that anyone tried to alert Zimbabwean authorities.

The record does not show whether the law on faith-based organisations was passed. Exploitation around mines is reported as continuing in 2025.

GBR.story:
The British record has three main parts: abuse in institutions that held or served children, groups of men who groomed and sexually exploited girls in English towns, and British men abusing children abroad or paying for abuse online.

In the grooming cases, men gave girls drink and drugs and passed them between themselves, and police and councils did not believe the girls. In Rotherham, children's-home managers and youth workers reported abuse from the 1990s, and a rape reported in 2001 ended with release without charge; the National Crime Agency has since identified about 1,150 potential victims and secured 39 convictions. A 2024 review in Rochdale found police had identified ringleaders in 2007 without pursuing them, and that senior police and council leaders left hundreds of children, mainly white girls from poor backgrounds abused by Asian men, "at the mercy" of gangs from 2004 to 2013. Oxfordshire's 2015 review estimated more than 350 victims and found police treated the girls as if they had chosen their situation.

In institutions, those in charge knew and protected the abuser or themselves. The Prisons Ombudsman found in 2025 that knowledge of abuse at Medomsley, a Home Office detention centre for young offenders, was "ignored and dismissed" by the Prison Service, police and Home Office. Fame and rank delayed action for decades. Jimmy Savile was first reported in 1958 and investigated twice by police in his lifetime without charge, and the BBC shelved a report on him in 2011. A pupil who reported the MP Cyril Smith in 1968 was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1992 Lambeth Palace, the Archbishop of Canterbury's office, passed police only the least incriminating of seven letters about Bishop Peter Ball. Evangelical leaders who received a 1982 report on John Smyth's beatings of boys kept it from police, and he moved to Zimbabwe. Claims of a protected "VIP ring" in Westminster, including Carl Beech's, were investigated and disproved.

Abroad, a 2003 law allows prosecution of offences against children overseas, but the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA), the national inquiry for England and Wales, counted only about eight successful prosecutions since 1997, among them Mark Frost, who abused boys from poor families in Thailand. The charity International Justice Mission says the UK is among the three largest consumers of livestreamed abuse of Filipino children. From 1869 to 1970, children in British care were sent to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia; IICSA found in 2018 that successive governments continued this despite evidence of sexual abuse.

Prosecutions of grooming networks continue, and the three-year deadline for civil abuse claims has been removed in Scotland (2017) and in England and Wales (2026).
